15640:
Sympathetic describes a person who understands and cares about another person's pain, sadness, or difficulty — and who shows that they care.

When you are sympathetic, you are not just aware that someone is suffering. You actually feel moved by it. You feel a pull in your heart toward that person. You want them to feel understood and less alone.

Example: Your friend just lost her job. You sit down with her, listen to how she feels, and say, "That must be really hard. I'm so sorry you're going through this." Your friend looks at you and says, "Thank you for being so sympathetic." She means that you made her feel heard and cared for.

A sympathetic person:

  • Listens without judging
  • Acknowledges the other person's pain as real and valid
  • Shows warmth and concern

You can be sympathetic through your words ("That sounds awful"), your expressions (a sympathetic nod, a sympathetic smile), or your actions (sitting with someone who is grieving).
The Second Meaning — Being "Sympathetic To" Something

When followed by "to", the word shifts slightly. "Sympathetic to" something means you support it, agree with it, or are open and favorable toward it — even if you are not personally suffering from it.

Example: "The judge was sympathetic to the prisoner's argument." This means the judge found the argument reasonable and was inclined to agree with it.

Example: "She is sympathetic to the idea of shorter working hours." She's not fully committed, but she sees value in the idea and leans toward supporting it.

This usage is very common in politics, law, and discussions about causes and beliefs. It signals leaning toward something, not necessarily full commitment.
The Third Meaning — A "Sympathetic Character" in Stories

In literature, film, and storytelling, a sympathetic character is one that the audience can feel for, root for, or emotionally connect with.

Here is the key insight: a sympathetic character does not have to be a good or kind person. It just means the audience understands why that character does what they do, and therefore feels something for them — concern, care, or even just interest.

Example: A story about a thief who steals to feed his sick child. He is doing something wrong, but he is a sympathetic character because readers understand his pain and desperation.

Example: "The author struggled to make the villain sympathetic." The author wanted readers to understand the villain's perspective — not to approve of him, but to feel something for him.
The Technical / Scientific Meaning

You will occasionally see "sympathetic" in scientific and medical contexts. The most important one:

The sympathetic nervous system is the part of your body's automatic control system that kicks in during stress, danger, or excitement — known as the "fight or flight" response. It speeds up your heart, sharpens your senses, and prepares your body to act fast. This usage is specialized and you will mostly encounter it in biology or medicine.

There is also sympathetic vibration (in physics) — when one object vibrates, a nearby object of the same natural frequency starts vibrating too, even without being touched directly. And sympathetic magic (in anthropology) — the folk belief that two things that resemble each other or were once connected can influence each other (like sticking pins in a doll to harm someone). These are niche uses, but worth knowing.
The Subtle Emotional Depth — What It Really Feels Like

Here is something important that many learners miss: being sympathetic does not mean you agree with someone or think they are right.

Example: "I was sympathetic toward him, even though I knew the mistake was his own fault." You can feel sorry for someone's pain without excusing what they did.

Also, sympathetic does not mean you have lived the same experience. It means you recognize and respect that the experience is painful for the other person.
How "Sympathetic" Differs From Similar Words

Sympathetic vs. Empathetic:
These are the two most commonly confused words in this space. The difference is about distance.

When you are sympathetic, you see someone's pain from the outside and feel concern for them. You are moved by their situation, but you remain yourself, looking in.

When you are empathetic, you go inside their experience — you feel what they feel, as though you are standing in their shoes. Empathy is deeper and more immersive.

Think of it this way: A doctor can be sympathetic toward every patient's pain without having had every illness themselves. But a fellow patient who has gone through the exact same surgery and says "I know exactly what you're feeling right now" — that is empathy.

Sympathetic vs. Compassionate:
Compassionate carries a stronger sense of wanting to help and relieve suffering. Compassion almost always has an action component. Sympathy is more about the feeling and expression of understanding; compassion is about the urge to do something about the pain.

Sympathetic vs. Kind:
Kind is a broader, lighter word — it means generally pleasant and generous in nature. You can be kind to strangers in small ways (holding a door open). "Sympathetic" is specifically about responding to someone's pain or difficulty.
What "Sympathetic" Is NOT

This is important to avoid mistakes.

Being sympathetic does not mean you are being pitying — treating someone as weak or lesser. Sympathy, when done right, is respectful. It says "I see your pain" not "I look down on you because of your pain."

It also does not mean being soft or letting someone off the hook. You can sympathize with someone while still holding them accountable.

And importantly: a "sympathetic" person is not the same as an "agreeable" or "pleasant" person. A judge can be tough and strict while still being sympathetic to a difficult case.
Common Phrases and Collocations

Here are the most natural ways this word is used:

  • A sympathetic ear — a listener who genuinely cares about what you're saying. "She always lends me a sympathetic ear."
  • A sympathetic smile / nod / look — a facial expression that shows you understand and care.
  • Sympathetic to a cause / idea / proposal — supporting or open to it.
  • A sympathetic character — one the audience can connect with emotionally.
  • Met with a sympathetic response — the reaction was understanding and supportive.
Degree and Intensity

Like most adjectives, "sympathetic" can be made stronger or weaker:

  • Stronger: very sympathetic, deeply sympathetic, extremely sympathetic, genuinely sympathetic
  • Weaker: a little sympathetic, somewhat sympathetic, not entirely unsympathetic (this last one is a gentle way of saying someone showed at least some understanding)
The Opposite

The most direct opposites of sympathetic are:

Unsympathetic — showing no understanding, care, or concern for someone's pain. "The manager was unsympathetic to her employees' concerns."

Indifferent — completely unmoved and uninterested. Stronger than unsympathetic.

Cold / harsh / dismissive — these describe the way an unsympathetic person tends to behave.
A Final Summary to Lock It In

Sympathetic most often means: understanding and caring about someone else's pain or difficulty, and showing that care. It can also mean being in favor of or open to an idea or cause, or (in stories) being a character the audience can emotionally connect with.

The golden thread running through all the meanings is this: something is pulling toward something else — a heart pulling toward another person's pain, a mind pulling toward an idea, an audience's emotions pulling toward a character.
15641:
Sympathy is the warm feeling of care, sorrow, or concern that you have for someone else who is going through pain, loss, or difficulty — even though you yourself are not going through it.

When you feel sympathy for someone, you are emotionally moved by their suffering. You feel for them. You wish their pain would go away. You want them to feel better. That emotional pull toward another person in their hard times is sympathy.

Your neighbour's house burns down. You feel a deep sadness for them, a strong concern for what they are going through. That feeling is sympathy.
The Key Idea: Feeling For Someone, Not With Them

This is the most important thing to understand about sympathy. When you feel sympathy, you are standing beside someone's pain, looking at it from the outside, and feeling moved by it. You feel for them.

This is different from empathy, which is often confused with sympathy. Empathy is when you step inside someone's experience — you actually imagine yourself in their position and feel what they are feeling. With empathy, you feel with them.

Think of it this way:

A friend tells you they just lost their job and are terrified about paying their bills.

Sympathy sounds like: "I'm so sorry. That sounds really hard. I hope things get better for you soon." You feel concern and sadness for them, but you are feeling it from your own position.

Empathy sounds like: "I can feel how scary that must be — like the ground has been pulled from under your feet." You are actively imagining yourself into their fear.

Sympathy is gentler and more natural in everyday life. It doesn't require you to have had the same experience. A person who has never lost a job can still feel sympathy for someone who has.
The Second Meaning: Agreement or Support for a Cause or Idea

Sympathy doesn't always have to be about a person's pain. It also means a feeling of agreement with, or support for, an idea, a cause, or a group of people — especially one that others might disagree with.

"She had sympathy for the protesters, even though she didn't join them."

This means she understood and agreed with what they were fighting for. She was emotionally on their side.

"The judge expressed sympathy with the argument but ultimately rejected it."

Here it means the judge found the argument understandable or reasonable, even if he didn't fully accept it.

In this sense, sympathy is about where your heart and mind lean. It is a quiet, internal alignment with someone's position or struggle.

When the word becomes "sympathies" (plural), it is most commonly used in two ways.

First, it is used as a formal expression of condolence — what you say or send to someone who has experienced a death or great loss.

"Please accept my deepest sympathies on the loss of your mother."

This is why you see "sympathy cards" in shops — cards sent to someone who has lost a loved one, expressing your sorrow for them.

Second, "sympathies" can refer to a person's general loyalties or inclinations — which side of an issue their feelings lean toward.

"His political sympathies were always with the working class."
"Her sympathies clearly lay with the underdog."
What Sympathy Feels Like in Real Life

Sympathy is not just a cold, distant acknowledgment that someone is suffering. It is a genuine emotional response. When you feel sympathy, there is usually a softening inside you — a kind of ache or tenderness on behalf of the other person.

You might feel sympathy for:

A child who is being bullied. A friend going through a painful divorce. A stranger you read about in the news who lost everything in a flood. A colleague dealing with a serious illness.

In none of these cases do you need to have experienced the same thing yourself. That is the beauty of sympathy — it is a human bridge that lets you emotionally reach toward someone whose experience is not your own.
Sympathy vs. Pity — A Subtle but Important Difference

Pity and sympathy are related, but they are not the same.

Pity tends to look down at someone. It can carry a sense of distance, or even superiority — "I feel sorry for that poor person." Pity can sometimes feel condescending, as though you see the other person as helpless or beneath your own situation.

Sympathy is warmer and more respectful. It does not look down — it looks across. You see someone struggling, and you genuinely care. There is no distance or superiority in it. Most people would rather receive sympathy than pity.

"She didn't want anyone's pity — but she was touched by the sympathy her friends showed her."

Here are natural ways the word "sympathy" appears in everyday English:

"I feel sympathy for her." — You care about what she is going through.
"He expressed his sympathy." — He showed or said that he cared.
"You have my deepest sympathy." — A formal, heartfelt expression of sorrow for someone's loss.
"Out of sympathy." — Because of the care or concern you feel. ("She stayed, out of sympathy.")
"In sympathy with." — In support of or agreement with. ("The workers went on strike in sympathy with their colleagues.")
"Sympathy card / sympathy flowers." — Things sent to someone after a bereavement.
"Win someone's sympathy." — To make someone feel care or support toward you.

Sympathy is the genuine feeling of sorrow, care, and concern you feel for another person who is suffering or struggling — or, more broadly, a feeling of support and agreement toward a cause or idea you find worthy.
15642:
A symptom is a sign that something is happening inside a person's body or mind — usually something that is wrong, unusual, or out of balance. Think of a symptom as your body's way of sending a message: "Hey, something here is not normal."

The most important thing to understand is that a symptom is something you feel or experience yourself. It comes from the inside. It is your personal, internal experience of something being off. A headache is a symptom. So is nausea, tiredness, dizziness, pain, itching, or sadness. Nobody else can feel these things for you — only you know they are there.

This is different from a sign, which is something a doctor can observe or measure from the outside — like a rash they can see on your skin, or a fever they can measure with a thermometer. In everyday English, people often use "symptom" and "sign" interchangeably, and that is perfectly fine. But in strict medical language, a symptom lives inside the patient's experience, while a sign lives in what others can observe.
The Medical Context (Where the Word Is Used Most)

In medicine, symptoms are the clues that help doctors figure out what is wrong with you. When you visit a doctor and describe what you have been feeling — pain in your chest, difficulty breathing, a constant cough — those are your symptoms. The doctor listens to them, takes them seriously, and uses them to narrow down what condition or disease you might have.

For example, a runny nose, a sore throat, and a mild fever are common symptoms of a cold. Chest pain, shortness of breath, and sweating can be symptoms of a heart attack. Each disease tends to come with its own recognizable set of symptoms, which is why doctors ask "What are you feeling?" before anything else.

A group of symptoms that consistently appear together and are associated with a particular condition is sometimes called a syndrome — which is essentially a recognized package of symptoms.

Outside of medicine, people use "symptom" in a wider sense to describe any sign or indication that a deeper problem exists — not just in bodies, but in societies, relationships, systems, and situations.

For example: "The rise in unemployment is a symptom of a struggling economy." Here, unemployment is not a disease, but the word "symptom" works perfectly because unemployment is the visible, felt sign of a deeper, underlying problem (the economy being in trouble).

Or: "His constant lying is a symptom of his insecurity." The lying is the outward sign; the insecurity is the root cause underneath.

This broader use always follows the same logic: the symptom is the thing you can observe or feel on the surface, and it points toward a deeper cause underneath.
Cause vs. Symptom — A Critical Distinction

One of the most important ideas attached to this word is the difference between a symptom and its cause. A symptom is never the root problem — it is the result or expression of the root problem.

If you have a headache, the headache is the symptom. The cause might be dehydration, stress, or high blood pressure. If you only treat the headache (with a painkiller) but ignore what is causing it, you are treating the symptom, not the cause. This phrase — treating the symptom rather than the cause — is a very common and important expression in both medicine and everyday life. It means you are dealing with the surface-level sign of a problem without addressing what is actually producing it.

Two closely related words you will often encounter are built from "symptom":

Symptomatic means showing or relating to symptoms. If a person is symptomatic, they are experiencing noticeable symptoms of a condition. It can also mean something is characteristic of or typical of a problem — as in, "His attitude is symptomatic of the whole company's culture."

Asymptomatic means having a condition but showing no symptoms at all. This is a very important concept in medicine. A person can be infected with a virus and be completely asymptomatic — feeling totally fine — while still being able to spread the disease to others. This is what made COVID-19 particularly tricky to control.
How to Use "Symptom" in a Sentence

The word is a countable noun, so it can be singular (a symptom) or plural (symptoms). Here are the most natural and common ways it is used:

In medicine, you will hear things like: "What symptoms are you experiencing?" / "The main symptoms of flu include fever and body aches." / "She showed no symptoms for the first week." / "The medication helps relieve the symptoms but does not cure the disease."

In broader use: "Corruption in politics is a symptom of a broken system." / "Violence in schools is often a symptom of neglect at home."
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

A symptom is a signal from the inside — something felt or experienced — that tells you (or a doctor, or an observer) that something deeper is going on. It is never the root cause itself; it always points toward the root cause. Whether we are talking about a body, a relationship, or a society, a symptom is the visible or felt expression of an underlying condition.
15643:
You cannot fully understand "symptomatic" without first being clear on what a symptom is, because the adjective is entirely built on that idea.

A symptom is a visible, outward sign that something is happening — usually something wrong — on the inside. Crucially, a symptom is not the problem itself. It is simply the way the problem reveals itself to the outside world.

When you catch a cold, your runny nose, sore throat, and tiredness are symptoms. They are not the cold. The cold is the actual infection happening in your body. The symptoms are just the signals the infection sends out. They are the messenger, not the message.

With that foundation, "symptomatic" becomes straightforward: something is symptomatic when it acts like a symptom — when it is a revealing sign of something else happening beneath the surface.

1. The Medical Meaning: Showing Signs of Illness

In medicine, a person is called symptomatic when they are actively showing outward signs of a disease or condition. If you test positive for an infection and you feel feverish, tired, or unwell, you are symptomatic — your body is visibly expressing the illness.

The opposite is asymptomatic: you carry the disease inside you but show absolutely no outward signs. You feel fine, you look fine, but the illness is still there. This distinction became widely discussed during the COVID-19 pandemic, because asymptomatic people could unknowingly spread the virus to others.

In medical language, you will also hear the phrases symptomatic relief and symptomatic treatment. These mean treating the outward signs of illness to make the patient more comfortable — without necessarily curing the underlying cause. A painkiller that eases a headache gives symptomatic relief. It quiets the signal, but does not fix whatever triggered it.

2. The Figurative Meaning: A Sign of Something Deeper

This is where the word becomes especially powerful and widely used — far beyond hospitals and clinics.

In everyday and formal language, when something is described as symptomatic of something else, the speaker is saying: "What you are seeing on the surface is not random or isolated. It is a clue — a revealing sign — of a much bigger, deeper reality underneath."

This meaning almost always follows one specific pattern: [something visible] is symptomatic of [something deeper].

Consider these examples:

"His constant lateness is symptomatic of a more general disregard for other people's time." The lateness is the surface sign. What it reveals — a deeper attitude — is the real story the word is pointing to.

"The frequent power cuts are symptomatic of decades of under-investment in the country's infrastructure." The power cuts are real and frustrating, but calling them symptomatic signals that they are not stand-alone problems. They are signs of a much larger, more serious failure hiding underneath.

"Violence in that school is symptomatic of a failure of leadership at every level." Again — the violence is what you can see, but the word directs your attention past it, toward the root cause.
The Key Insight: The Symptom Is Never the Root Problem

The most important idea this word carries is this: whatever is described as symptomatic is the evidence of a problem, not the problem itself.

This logic works identically in both the medical and figurative uses. In medicine, if you only treat a symptom and ignore the underlying cause, the disease keeps going. You might feel temporarily better, but nothing is truly fixed. The same logic applies in its figurative use. When a writer or speaker calls something symptomatic, they are quietly arguing: do not stop at what you can see — look at what it reveals, because that is where the real issue lives.

This is also why the word carries a slightly serious, analytical, and sometimes critical tone. Using it is a way of saying that the visible problem is not the whole story, and perhaps not even the most important part of the story.

In practice, "symptomatic" almost always appears with the word of right after it. This is its natural partner.

The full pattern: [Visible thing] is symptomatic of [deeper thing].

You will sometimes see "symptomatic" used without "of" — typically in medical contexts — and it simply means "showing symptoms." For example, "the patient became symptomatic on day four" or "symptomatic cases were sent for testing." Here, there is no "of" because the deeper illness is already understood.
Does It Always Signal Something Bad?

Almost always, yes. The word almost exclusively gravitates toward negative, problematic, or worrying situations. Symptoms in medicine are signs of disease, and the figurative use carries that same shadow. You call a trouble symptomatic — a warning sign, a red flag, a tell.

While it is not grammatically wrong to use it for something positive (such as "her warmth is symptomatic of a generous spirit"), it would sound unusual and slightly awkward. The word simply belongs to the world of problems, failures, and things that deserve a closer, more critical look.

Symptomatic (adjective) means being a visible sign or indication of something else. In medicine, it describes a person or condition that is showing outward signs of a disease, as opposed to being asymptomatic (showing none). More broadly and figuratively, it describes something that is a revealing clue — a surface-level sign pointing to a deeper problem, pattern, or failure. The word always invites you to look past what you can see and ask: what does this tell us about what is really going on beneath?
15644: A synagogue is a Jewish house of worship — a building where Jewish people gather to pray, study their sacred texts, and come together as a community. Think of it the way a church is to Christians, or a mosque is to Muslims. It serves the same fundamental role: a dedicated, sacred space for a religious community to meet, practice their faith, and connect with one another.
What Actually Happens Inside a Synagogue?

A synagogue is not just a place for prayer. It has three main purposes, and all three are equally important:

1. Prayer. Jewish people gather in the synagogue for worship services, especially on the Sabbath (the Jewish day of rest, which runs from Friday evening to Saturday night), and on Jewish holidays. The prayers are often recited in Hebrew, the ancient and sacred language of the Jewish people.

2. Study. The synagogue is a place of learning. Jewish teachings, religious law, and sacred scripture — particularly the Torah (the first five books of the Hebrew Bible) — are studied and discussed here. This makes it, in many ways, a school as much as a place of worship.

3. Community gathering. A synagogue is a social and cultural hub for the Jewish community. Life events like bar and bat mitzvahs (coming-of-age ceremonies for Jewish boys and girls), weddings, and memorial services often take place here. It is where a Jewish community stays connected and supports each other.
What Does a Synagogue Look Like Inside?

While synagogues can look very different on the outside depending on the country and era they were built in, they typically share certain features on the inside:

  • The Ark (Aron Kodesh): A cabinet or alcove at the front of the hall where the Torah scrolls — handwritten on parchment and considered extremely sacred — are stored. The congregation faces the Ark during prayer.
  • The Bimah: A raised platform, usually in the center or at the front of the hall, where the Torah is read aloud to the congregation.
  • The Ner Tamid: A lamp or light that hangs above the Ark and is kept burning at all times. It symbolizes the eternal presence of God.
  • Seating: Rows of seats for the congregation to sit during services.

Some synagogues are grand and architecturally stunning. Others are simple and modest rooms. The size and style depend heavily on the community's resources and traditions.

The rabbi is the main religious and spiritual leader of a synagogue. The word "rabbi" means "teacher" in Hebrew, which tells you a lot — their role is as much about teaching and guiding the community as it is about leading prayers. A cantor (also called a hazzan) is a trained vocalist who leads the congregation in singing the prayers and hymns during services.

No. Just as there are different branches of Christianity (Catholic, Protestant, etc.), there are different movements within Judaism, and each has its own style of synagogue:

  • Orthodox synagogues follow traditional Jewish law very strictly. Men and women sit separately during services, and prayers are conducted almost entirely in Hebrew.
  • Conservative synagogues maintain many traditions but allow for some adaptations to modern life.
  • Reform synagogues take a more modern, flexible approach. Services may be conducted partly in the local language (like English), and men and women sit together.

Despite these differences, all synagogues share the same core identity: a place for Jewish worship, learning, and community.
One Sentence to Remember It By

If you ever need to recall this word quickly, just remember: a synagogue is the Jewish equivalent of a church or a mosque — but it is also a school and a community center all rolled into one building.
15645: A synapse is a tiny junction — a point of communication — between two nerve cells (called neurons), or between a neuron and another type of cell (like a muscle cell). It is the place where a signal from one cell is passed on to the next. The word is used as a countable noun: you can have a synapse, many synapses, this synapse.

Your nervous system is built from billions of neurons. These neurons form long chains and networks to carry information — from your eyes to your brain, from your brain to your muscles, and everywhere in between. But here's the key fact: neurons don't physically touch each other. There is always a tiny gap between them. That gap, along with the structures on either side of it, is the synapse. The synapse is nature's solution to the problem of passing a signal across that gap.

A synapse has three parts:

  1. The presynaptic terminal — the "sending" end. This is the tip of the neuron that is sending the signal. It contains tiny sacs called vesicles, which are filled with chemical messengers.
  2. The synaptic cleft — the gap itself. It is unimaginably small, about 20–40 nanometres wide (a nanometre is one billionth of a metre). Yet this tiny gap is where the magic of communication happens.
  3. The postsynaptic membrane — the "receiving" end. This is the surface of the next neuron (or cell), and it is studded with receptors — special protein structures that are designed to detect and respond to the chemical messengers from the other side.

Signals travel through a neuron as electrical impulses. When an electrical impulse reaches the presynaptic terminal, it triggers the vesicles there to release their chemical messengers into the synaptic cleft. These chemical messengers are called neurotransmitters.

The neurotransmitters float across the cleft and bind to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane — like a key fitting into a lock. When a neurotransmitter binds to its receptor, it causes a reaction in the receiving cell. Depending on the type of neurotransmitter and receptor involved, this reaction either:

  • Excites the next neuron — meaning it encourages that neuron to fire its own electrical signal and pass the message along, or
  • Inhibits the next neuron — meaning it suppresses that neuron from firing, essentially putting a brake on the signal.

After the neurotransmitters do their job, they are either broken down by enzymes in the cleft, or they are taken back up into the presynaptic neuron to be reused. This cleanup process is called reuptake.

There are two main types:

Chemical synapses are the most common type, and they work exactly as described above — using neurotransmitters to carry the signal across the gap. They are slightly slower (a tiny fraction of a millisecond delay) because the signal has to convert from electrical to chemical and back to electrical.

Electrical synapses are less common. Here, the two cells are connected through protein channels called gap junctions, and the electrical signal passes directly from one cell to the other with no chemical step. These are faster but allow less control over the signal.

Since neurotransmitters are central to how synapses work, it helps to know the major ones:

  • Glutamate — the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter; it promotes the firing of signals and is crucial for learning and memory.
  • GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) — the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter; it calms neural activity and prevents overstimulation.
  • Dopamine — involved in pleasure, reward, motivation, and movement.
  • Serotonin — regulates mood, sleep, appetite, and emotional balance.
  • Acetylcholine — vital for muscle movement and also important in memory and attention.
  • Norepinephrine — involved in alertness, the stress response, and the "fight or flight" reaction.

One of the most remarkable things about synapses is that they are not fixed. They can grow stronger or weaker over time based on how often they are used. This ability is called synaptic plasticity, and it is the biological foundation of learning and memory.

When two neurons repeatedly fire together — when a synapse is used over and over — it becomes more efficient. The connection strengthens: the presynaptic terminal releases more neurotransmitter, and the postsynaptic membrane grows more receptors. This is often summarised as "neurons that fire together, wire together."

Conversely, synapses that are rarely or never used weaken and can eventually disappear — a process called synaptic pruning. This is not a failure; it is the brain being efficient, removing connections it no longer needs. A lot of pruning happens during childhood and adolescence as the brain refines itself.

The formation of a new memory, the learning of a new skill, or even a habit you develop — all of these are, at the physical level, changes in synaptic strength and structure.
How many synapses does a human brain have?

The human brain is estimated to contain roughly 100 trillion synapses. That is more than all the stars in the Milky Way galaxy. This staggering number gives you a sense of the complexity of the brain's communication network — and why the brain is capable of such remarkable things.

Because synapses are the communication points of the entire nervous system, disruptions at the synapse have profound consequences. Many neurological and psychiatric conditions are, at their core, problems with synaptic function:

  • Parkinson's disease involves the death of neurons that produce dopamine, leading to fewer dopamine synapses in brain regions that control movement.
  • Depression is linked in part to reduced signalling at serotonin and norepinephrine synapses.
  • Alzheimer's disease involves the destruction of synapses in brain regions responsible for memory, which is why memory loss is its hallmark symptom.
  • Epilepsy involves uncontrolled, excessive firing across synapses in the brain.
  • Myasthenia gravis is a condition where the immune system attacks acetylcholine receptors at the synapses between neurons and muscle cells, causing muscle weakness.

Many medications work directly at synapses. Antidepressants like SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) block the reuptake of serotonin, keeping it in the synaptic cleft longer so it can have a stronger effect. Drugs like caffeine, nicotine, opioids, and many anaesthetics also work by interfering with synaptic signalling in specific ways.

If you had to capture the essence of the word in one sentence: a synapse is the specialised junction between neurons where the nervous system's electrical signals are converted into chemical messages and passed from one cell to the next — and in doing so, it makes possible every thought you think, every movement you make, every memory you hold, and every emotion you feel.
15646:
Synchronicity is the experience of two or more events happening around the same time that have no logical cause-and-effect connection to each other, yet feel deeply and meaningfully related.

Notice the two key ingredients baked into that definition:

No causal link. Neither event caused the other. They happened independently.

Yet a meaningful connection. The match between them feels too significant, too perfect, too striking to simply brush off as a random accident.

That tension — "these events are unconnected, and yet..." — is the heart of synchronicity.

You haven't thought about your grandmother in months. Then, on a random Tuesday morning, her face pops into your mind for no particular reason. Ten minutes later, your phone rings. It's her.

Neither event caused the other. Your thought didn't make her call. Her decision to call didn't trigger your thought. And yet the two events lined up in a way that feels loaded with meaning — like the universe quietly arranged them.

That is synchronicity.
How It Differs From a Regular Coincidence

This is the most important distinction to understand, because the two words are often confused.

A coincidence is simply two things happening around the same time — full stop. There's no deeper layer to it. If two strangers happen to wear the same shirt to a party, that's a coincidence. Mildly funny. Easily forgotten.

Synchronicity goes further. It's a coincidence that carries weight — one that feels personally significant, almost as if it were arranged or pointed at you for a reason. It's not just "oh, funny timing" — it's "that timing means something."

Think of it this way: all synchronicities involve coincidence, but not all coincidences feel like synchronicity. Synchronicity is a coincidence with a sense of meaning attached to it.
Where the Word Comes From (Conceptually, Not Historically)

The Swiss psychiatrist Carl Jung is the person who gave this word its formal definition and brought it into the wider world. He spent years observing moments in his patients' lives — and his own — where an inner event (a thought, a dream, a strong feeling) would align uncannily with an outer event (something happening in the physical world) at the same time, with no causal link between them.

He believed these moments weren't just random noise. He thought they pointed to a hidden layer of connection in the world — a kind of invisible thread linking inner experience and outer reality — that science couldn't explain through cause and effect alone. He called this an acausal connecting principle, meaning: a force or pattern that connects things not through cause and effect, but through meaning.

You don't need to agree with Jung's interpretation to understand or use the word. But knowing this background helps you feel why the word carries such weight. It was never meant to describe a trivial coincidence. It was meant to describe a moment that makes you pause and ask: "Is the world trying to tell me something?"

In practice, you'll hear the word used across a spectrum — from the very precise to the very casual.

In its strict, original sense, synchronicity refers specifically to a meaningful coincidence between an inner psychological experience (a thought, emotion, intuition, or dream) and an outer event in the world, where neither caused the other.

Example: You dream about a plane crash, feel unsettled all morning, and then hear news of an actual aviation accident later that day. There's no way your dream caused the crash or that the crash caused your dream. Yet they aligned. That strict, Jungian meaning is what the word was originally built for.

In everyday, casual usage, people stretch the word a little more loosely to describe any striking, meaningful coincidence — even between two external events, not necessarily one internal and one external.

Example: Two old friends, living in different countries, both independently decide to write each other a letter on the exact same day, and the letters cross in the mail. Neither one triggered the other. It feels uncanny. People would call this synchronicity too.

Both uses are widely accepted. The strict use is more precise; the casual use is more common.

It is not the same as things happening simultaneously. Two clocks showing the same time is synchrony — not synchronicity. Synchrony is purely about timing. Synchronicity requires a felt sense of meaning on top of the timing.

It is not cause and effect. If you study hard and pass your exam, that's not synchronicity — that's your effort causing an outcome. Synchronicity specifically describes events with no such cause-and-effect chain between them.

It is not necessarily supernatural. Many people experience synchronicity as a spiritual or mystical phenomenon, and that's a valid personal interpretation. But the word itself doesn't demand a supernatural explanation. Some people see synchronicities as meaningful patterns produced by the mind's tendency to find connections. Others see them as genuine signals from the universe. The word accommodates both views — it describes the experience without insisting on a single explanation for it.

To cement your understanding, here's how the word appears in real contexts:

"After losing his job, he met his future business partner in a random elevator — a synchronicity he never stopped talking about."

"She didn't believe in fate, but the synchronicity of receiving a job offer on the exact day she'd decided to quit was hard to ignore."

"Jung spent his career studying synchronicity — those strange, meaningful coincidences that logic alone cannot fully account for."

"The synchronicity of their thoughts — both writing the same idea in their notebooks on the same night, miles apart — felt almost eerie."

If you ever need to compress the word to its simplest form:

Synchronicity is a meaningful coincidence — two unconnected events that align in a way that feels significant, as if shaped by something beyond chance.

Hold that definition, layer in the nuances above, and you have a complete, lifelong understanding of the word.
15647:
To synchronize means to make two or more things match up perfectly — in timing, in data, or in action — so that they are always in agreement with each other.

The key word here is match. When things are synchronized, they are not just similar or close — they are in precise alignment. Nothing is ahead. Nothing is behind. Nothing is different from what the other has.
The Two Main Flavors of Meaning

This single word carries two slightly different but closely related meanings depending on how it is used.

Flavor 1: To make things happen at exactly the same time.

This is about timing. If you synchronize two events, you arrange them so they occur at the precise same moment — not one before the other, not slightly off, but simultaneously.

Example: Two people in different cities need to open a door at exactly the same second. They synchronize — they coordinate so their actions happen at the same instant.

Flavor 2: To make two things match each other's current state, so they are identical or consistent.

This is about matching content or status, not just timing. Here, you are not necessarily making things happen at the same time — you are making sure that what one thing has or shows is the same as what another thing has or shows.

Example: You edit a document on your phone. Later, you synchronize your phone with your laptop, which means the laptop now has the updated version too. Both devices now show the same thing. They are in agreement.

Imagine two clocks hanging on two different walls. One shows 3:00. The other shows 3:07. They are out of sync — they disagree. Now you adjust one until both show exactly 3:00. You have just synchronized them.

Now take that same idea and stretch it beyond just clocks — you can synchronize music, movements, files, systems, machines, teams, or schedules. The core act is always the same: you bring two or more things into agreement so that they match perfectly and move forward together.
How It Is Used in Different Situations

In everyday life:
When a group of swimmers performs a routine together — every arm movement, every dip, every turn happening in unison — their movements are synchronized. If one person is even a second early or late, the synchronization is broken.

In technology:
When your phone synchronizes with a cloud service, it means your phone sends its latest data to the cloud, and the cloud sends any updates back to your phone, so both now hold the exact same information. Neither is outdated. Neither is missing anything the other has.

In audio and video:
When you watch a video and the actor's lips move perfectly in time with the words you hear, the audio and video are synchronized. If you've ever watched a video where the voice and lips don't match up, that is a loss of synchronization — commonly called being "out of sync."

In the workplace:
When two teams working on the same project synchronize, they share updates, align their progress, and make sure no one is working with outdated information or going in a different direction.
What It Means to Be "Out of Sync"

Understanding the opposite helps sharpen the meaning. When things are out of sync, they have drifted apart — one has moved ahead, one has fallen behind, or one has changed while the other hasn't. To synchronize is to correct that drift and bring them back into alignment.
Important Nuance: It Is an Active Process

Synchronization does not happen by accident. To synchronize is a deliberate action — someone (or some system) actively makes it happen. Two clocks on opposite sides of the world will drift apart over time. Left alone, they go out of sync. Someone has to step in and synchronize them.

This is why the word carries a sense of effort and intention. You are not just noticing that two things match — you are making them match.

Synchronization can refer to a one-time act or an ongoing process.

A one-time act: "We synchronized our watches before the mission." It happened once, at that moment.

An ongoing process: Your email app constantly synchronizes in the background, pulling in new messages and updating in real time, so what you see always reflects the latest state of things.

To synchronize means to deliberately bring two or more things into perfect alignment — either so they happen at exactly the same time, or so they hold the same information or state — ensuring that nothing is ahead, behind, or out of agreement.
15648:
Synchronized describes two or more things that are perfectly coordinated in time, pace, or state — meaning they move together, happen together, or match each other exactly, as though they are operating as one unified whole.

The simplest way to grasp it: imagine two clocks on a wall, both showing 3:47:22 at the exact same moment. They are synchronized — they agree perfectly on time, right down to the second. Neither is ahead. Neither is behind. They match.

The word captures something deeper than just "happening at the same time." It carries the idea of deliberate coordination or alignment — things that have been arranged, designed, or adjusted so that they correspond to each other perfectly.

Think of it in three layers:

1. Same timing — Multiple things happen at exactly the same moment.
2. Same pace — Multiple things move or change at exactly the same rate, keeping up with each other.
3. Same state — Multiple things are updated or adjusted so that their contents, settings, or information match.

A single word can carry any one of these meanings — or sometimes all three at once — depending on context.

In sports:
In synchronized swimming, a team of athletes performs the same movements — the same kick, the same arm raise, the same spin — at precisely the same moment. If one person moves a half-second later than the rest, the synchronization is broken. The beauty of the performance comes entirely from how perfectly matched the timing is.

Similarly, in synchronized diving, two divers jump from the platform at the same instant and execute the same twists and flips in the air simultaneously. Judges score how closely their movements mirror each other.

In timekeeping:
Soldiers before a mission "synchronize their watches" — they all set their watches to the exact same time so that when one person says "attack at 0600," everyone's clock agrees on when that moment is. Without synchronized watches, one person's 6:00 a.m. might be another's 5:58 a.m., creating dangerous confusion.

In technology:
When your phone and laptop are synchronized, it means the data on both devices matches. If you add an appointment to your calendar on your phone, a synchronized system automatically updates your laptop's calendar too — both now contain the same information. Neither device is "behind."

Similarly, your music app stays synchronized across devices: the song you paused at 2:34 on your phone appears paused at 2:34 when you open the app on your computer.

In film and audio:
When you watch a video and the sound matches the picture perfectly — you hear the door slam at exactly the moment the door closes on screen — the audio and video are synchronized. When they are not synchronized (a common technical glitch), you'll hear someone speak before or after their mouth moves, which feels deeply unsettling.

In machines and engineering:
Gears inside an engine are synchronized — they mesh and turn together in a precisely timed relationship. A "synchronized gearbox" in a car allows the gears to match their rotational speeds before engaging, making gear shifts smooth rather than grinding.

In music:
When an orchestra performs, every musician plays in a synchronized rhythm — their beats align together under the conductor's guidance. If a single musician plays slightly off time, the whole piece sounds disjointed.

In nature:
Fireflies in certain parts of the world flash in synchronized patterns — thousands of them blink on and off at the exact same moment, as if controlled by a single switch. Scientists have studied this as a natural example of synchronization emerging without any central coordinator.
The Crucial Nuance: How Is "Synchronized" Different From "Simultaneous"?

This is the distinction that sharpens your understanding.

Simultaneous simply means two things happen at the same time — but by coincidence or by chance. Right now, millions of people are blinking simultaneously. A dog barking and a car horn honking at the same instant are simultaneous. There is no connection between them; they just happened to coincide.

Synchronized, on the other hand, means the timing is intentional, coordinated, and interdependent. The things are aligned with each other — they are in a relationship of matching. Synchronized swimmers aren't just accidentally moving their arms at the same moment; they have rehearsed and adjusted their movements specifically to match one another.

In short: simultaneous is about the same moment. Synchronized is about being coordinated and in harmony with each other.

Another way to feel this: "simultaneous" is a neutral description of timing. "Synchronized" carries a sense of achievement, design, or precision — something has been brought into alignment.
The Opposite: What "Out of Sync" Looks Like

Understanding the opposite makes the word click.

When things are not synchronized, they are described as out of sync, unsynchronized, or asynchronous. This creates mismatch, confusion, or disruption:

  • Swimmers out of sync look chaotic — arms flying at different moments, the formation collapsed.
  • An audio track out of sync with video looks eerie and wrong — lips moving in silence, then sound arriving late.
  • Clocks that are out of sync lead to missed appointments and failed coordination.
  • Data that isn't synchronized means your phone shows one version of a document and your laptop shows an older, different version — leading to errors and conflicts.

The discomfort you feel when things are out of sync is itself a proof of how natural and expected synchronization feels. When it works, it's invisible. When it breaks, everything feels off.

Synchronization is not always all-or-nothing. Things can be:

  • Perfectly synchronized — the match is exact, with zero deviation.
  • Closely synchronized — nearly matching, with only tiny differences.
  • Loosely synchronized — roughly coordinated, but not perfectly timed.
  • Poorly synchronized — attempted coordination that failed to align well.

For example, two musicians playing together might be "loosely synchronized" — playing the same song at roughly the same tempo, but with slight timing differences. A metronome-driven recording session achieves "perfect synchronization."
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

• "The two dancers moved in synchronized steps, never missing a beat."
  • "Make sure your team's calendars are synchronized before the meeting."
  • "The synchronized flashing of the warning lights guided traffic safely."
  • "The divers executed a synchronized entry into the water, barely making a splash."
  • "The backup system uses synchronized copies of data to prevent any loss."
  • "Their movements were so synchronized that the audience gasped."

Notice that in every case, "synchronized" tells you that multiple elements are in a coordinated, matched relationship — not just coincidentally happening together, but deliberately or functionally aligned.

If you had to remember one thing: synchronized means brought into perfect agreement — in time, in pace, in rhythm, or in content. It describes things that have been aligned so carefully that they behave as a unified, harmonious whole rather than as separate, independent pieces.

The moment you see the word, your brain should picture two or more things moving in perfect lockstep — no one ahead, no one behind, no one out of step. That image, in whatever context the word appears, is exactly what "synchronized" means.
15649:
Synchronous describes things that happen at the same time, or that operate in perfectly matched, coordinated timing with each other.

The heart of the word is shared time. Two or more things are synchronous when they are locked together in time — moving in step, running together, or occurring at the same moment in a deliberate, coordinated way.

A simple image to hold in your head: imagine two metronomes ticking at exactly the same beat, perfectly aligned. Neither is ahead or behind the other. That is synchronous.

Here is the key question to ask: Do these things require real-time coordination with each other — must they happen together, in step?

If yes → they are synchronous.
If no → they are asynchronous (the opposite).

Notice that "synchronous" implies more than a coincidence of timing. It implies an ongoing, sustained alignment — things that are deliberately or naturally designed to move together in time, not just two things that happen to occur at the same moment by chance.

A phone call is synchronous. Both people are present at the same moment. You speak, they hear you right then, they respond, you hear them right then. The entire conversation requires both parties to be in the same moment in time together.

A text message, by contrast, is asynchronous. You send it now. They might read it in three hours and reply tomorrow. No shared real-time moment is required.

A live concert is synchronous — the musicians and the audience share the same moment together.

A recorded podcast is asynchronous — the speaker recorded it on a Tuesday; you listen on a Friday. Both sides of the exchange exist at entirely different points in time.

A live classroom is synchronous — teacher and students are all present at the same time.

A self-paced online course is asynchronous — you take it whenever you want, at your own pace.

You will almost always see "synchronous" used alongside or in contrast to its opposite — asynchronous — so understanding the contrast is essential.

SynchronousAsynchronous

Synchronous = must happen at the same time, in step, in real-time coordination.

Asynchronous = does not require shared timing; things happen independently, at their own pace.

The simplest way to feel the difference: a phone call is synchronous, an email is asynchronous. Both are forms of communication, but one demands that both people exist in the same moment; the other does not.

This is the domain where "synchronous" is used most carefully and precisely today, so it deserves a thorough explanation.

In computing, a synchronous process is one where each step must wait for the previous step to fully finish before it can begin. The program moves forward in strict order, one step at a time, and nothing proceeds until the current step is done.

Picture a single toll booth on a road. Cars must stop, pay, and only then pass through. The next car cannot move until the car ahead has cleared the booth. One at a time, in order, no skipping ahead. That is a synchronous process.

A real example: if a computer program downloads a file synchronously, the entire program freezes and waits — doing absolutely nothing else — until that file is completely downloaded. Only after the download is 100% complete does the program move on to its next instruction.

An asynchronous process works the opposite way. The program starts the download and then immediately continues doing other things — maybe updating the screen, responding to your clicks, running other calculations — while the download happens quietly in the background. When the download eventually finishes, the program is notified and handles it.

So in computing:

  • Synchronous = sequential, step-by-step, each step blocks everything else until it's done.
  • Asynchronous = tasks can run independently and in parallel, without waiting for each other.

This distinction matters enormously in software. Modern websites and apps are heavily asynchronous because blocking everything while waiting for one slow task (like a network request) would make the experience feel frozen and terrible. But synchronous code is simpler to write and reason about, because you always know exactly what order things happen in.

In astronomy and physics, "synchronous" appears in a beautiful and precise way.

A synchronous orbit is when a satellite orbits a planet at exactly the same rate as the planet itself rotates. The result: the satellite appears to hover perfectly still above one fixed point on the planet's surface, never drifting.

The satellites that power your TV dish, weather forecasts, and some GPS systems are in geostationary orbit around Earth — a type of synchronous orbit. They orbit Earth once every 24 hours, exactly matching Earth's own rotation. So from the ground, they look like they're not moving at all.

The Moon is another remarkable example. The Moon rotates on its own axis in almost exactly the same time it takes to orbit Earth. This is called synchronous rotation. The result: we on Earth always see the exact same face of the Moon. The "far side of the Moon" is permanently facing away from us — not because it doesn't rotate, but because its rotation is perfectly synchronized with its orbit.

A synchronous motor is an electric motor whose rotational speed is precisely locked to the frequency of the electrical power supply feeding it. If the power supply runs at 60 Hz (cycles per second), the motor spins at a rate directly tied to those 60 cycles. It stays synchronized with the electrical current. This makes synchronous motors extremely precise and predictable — useful in clocks, timekeeping devices, and situations where exact speed matters.
The Subtle Nuance: It's Always About Time

No matter which field you encounter this word in, the core concept never changes. "Synchronous" is always about time alignment.

  • Two events: do they occur at the same moment?
  • Two people communicating: must they be present at the same time?
  • Two processes in a computer: does one wait for the other before proceeding?
  • A satellite and a planet: do they move at the same rate?

Whenever you see "synchronous," ask: what two (or more) things are in time-step with each other, and how? The answer will always be the meaning.

Synchronous (adjective): happening at the same time; operating in coordinated, matched timing; requiring or exhibiting real-time alignment between two or more things.

Its opposite is asynchronous: not happening at the same time; not requiring shared timing; able to operate independently.

The word appears in everyday language (live calls, live events), in computing (step-by-step processes that wait for each other), in astronomy (orbits that match a planet's rotation), and in engineering (motors locked to an electrical frequency). In every case, it is about things moving together in time — in step, in coordination, locked to the same clock.
